translations: She still kept her secret identity because the studies weren't finished yet, and revealing it would cause trouble for both her and the academy. Liang Shanbo never took advantage of her alone time to pry into her personal life. He genuinely treated her like a trusted brother, never crossing any boundaries to investigate.

With graduation still a ways off, letters from home began to urge Zhu Yingtai to return. Her father said the agreed-upon time limit had passed, and there were other arrangements at home. She folded the letter without immediately telling Liang Shanbo, wanting to spend the last few days of their time together as usual.

Aman noticed they were talking less and less, so he stopped making jokes. He wrote on a green bamboo slip: "Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai have been classmates for many years, helping and understanding each other; Liang Shanbo still doesn't know Zhu Yingtai's true identity."
Soon, the separation forced Zhu Yingtai to hide her true feelings in a long, sentimental goodbye.
Her father kept urging her to return, and Zhu Yingtai finally packed her books.

Liang Shanbo insisted on accompanying her. Zhu Yingtai said the mountain road was long, and he could send her to the ferry; Liang Shanbo, however, walked with her from the academy gate, passing through one pavilion after another, never turning back. This stretch of road would later be called the "Eighteen Goodbyes."
As they passed by a pond, a pair of swans swam together. Zhu Yingtai said, "In the water, the birds are always in pairs; Liang Shanbo, what do you think of them?"
Liang Shanbo looked carefully and said, "The one on the left is swimming faster."
Zhu Yingtai waited a moment and said, "You only noticed which one was faster?"
Liang Shanbo replied, "I also noticed they weren't afraid of the water."
Zhu Yingtai swallowed the next line of her poem, thinking the swans had done their best for the day.

As they passed by a small bridge, the butterflies on the bridge were chasing each other. Zhu Yingtai said, "The butterflies are a pair, and they don't want to be separated." Liang Shanbo replied, "It's spring, and the flowers are many; the butterflies naturally come." She then pointed to the reflection of a man and a woman in the well, but Liang Shanbo was worried she was thirsty and turned to fetch water.

Liang Shanbo lowered the well rope, and the bucket hit the well wall twice before falling into the water. As he lifted the bucket, he was so focused on not spilling water that he didn't notice the rope was tangled around his sleeve, and when he lifted his arm, it was stretched out horizontally in the air. Zhu Yingtai helped him untangle the rope, saying, "You were just like the man and woman in the reflection – you tied yourself to the rope."
"At least the rope understands that it needs to help lift the water," Liang Shanbo said, handing her a water dipper. "If I miss something, you can just explain it clearly to me."

The opportunity came suddenly, and Zhu Yingtai almost said, "I'm a woman." But there were people passing by on the bridge, and they were still close to the academy. If she revealed her true identity on the road, Liang Shanbo might not have time to hear her out before her secret was discovered by the academy. So she changed her words, saying, "I have a younger sister at home, and she's similar to me in character and learning. If you meet her, you might not need me to explain anything."

Liang Shanbo took this as a serious request and asked about her younger sister's studies, interests, and whether she had been promised to anyone. Zhu Yingtai saw that he was finally on the right track and felt a glimmer of hope, but then he asked, "If she's similar to you, does she often say half of what she means, leaving the other half for people to guess?"
Zhu Yingtai handed him the water dipper, saying, "That's especially similar."

They continued on their way. As they passed by a small temple, the statues on the roof were a pair of people sitting together. Zhu Yingtai said, "If two people know each other, even if they have simple clothes and food, they can still be together for a long time." Liang Shanbo nodded in agreement, but then he noticed that one of the statues had a hat that was half-broken, and he carefully placed a large leaf over it to protect it from the rain. Zhu Yingtai watched him and felt both amused and more confident that he would respect her "younger sister."

As they reached the next pavilion, she decided to make her hint more explicit, saying, "If my younger sister wants to marry someone who has been a classmate for many years, is honest, and only takes a little time to understand her, would you be willing to visit her?" Liang Shanbo finally understood that this was an invitation to propose, and his face turned red as he replied, "If she truly wants to, I'll certainly visit her seriously. However, marriage is a big decision, and I want to hear her say it herself, not just rely on her brother's agreement."

Zhu Yingtai heard the words "hear her say it herself" and felt her heart lift a little. She couldn't reveal her true identity yet, so she asked him to visit her family soon. Liang Shanbo asked about the address and etiquette, even thinking about what kind of books to bring as a gift. Zhu Yingtai smiled at him, saying he was finally not just thinking about farming, and Liang Shanbo replied, "If I fix the plow wrong, I can adjust it again, but if I say something wrong when visiting, I'm afraid I'll be remembered by your family for a lifetime."

The laughter in their goodbyes came from their finally being close to the same understanding, but it also made their later misunderstandings more poignant. Zhu Yingtai had tried to convey her feelings to him as much as possible, and Liang Shanbo had agreed to visit her family; however, they didn't know that another marriage proposal had already arrived at her family's doorstep.

Zhu Yingtai's hints began to shift from paired scenery to marriage. She asked Liang Shanbo what kind of woman he would want to marry, and he replied that he wanted someone intelligent, kind, and honest, who could speak her mind.

As they walked through a field, they saw a mother cow and her calf, with the farmer and his wife working together to plow the land. Zhu Yingtai used the scene to say that if a family works together, even poverty can be better than living in luxury alone. Liang Shanbo nodded, saying, "If a couple knows each other, it's more important than matching social status."
Zhu Yingtai asked him what he would do if the woman spoke her mind first, and Liang Shanbo replied, "If she truly speaks her mind, I should take her seriously and not mock her."
"What if she had been hiding her true identity from you?" Zhu Yingtai asked.
"If she had a good reason to hide, I should listen to her explanation first," Liang Shanbo said.

As they walked, Zhu Yingtai almost revealed her true identity, but a group of porters passed by on the narrow road, forcing them to let each other pass. By the time they were side by side again, Liang Shanbo was talking about the plow, analyzing why it was too shallow in the ground. Zhu Yingtai sighed, saying, "If you were to be a matchmaker, people might have to learn to plow the land first."
Liang Shanbo replied, "I might not be a good matchmaker, but I can try fixing the plow."

Zhu Yingtai suppressed a smile, feeling more confident that Liang Shanbo wasn't taking her hints lightly, but she also realized that he had no idea that the "Zhu brother" he was talking to was actually her.
"What if the person you're talking about is right in front of you?" Zhu Yingtai asked.
Liang Shanbo looked ahead, thinking she was referring to a village girl on the road: "I don't know her, so I wouldn't dare to be forward."
Zhu Yingtai felt both anger and sadness. Liang Shanbo's slowness had ruined her hints, but his integrity was exactly what she valued.

As they reached the next pavilion, Zhu Yingtai couldn't walk with him any further. She finally revealed that she had a younger sister who looked and acted like her, and if Liang Shanbo was interested, he could visit her family soon. This "younger sister" was the most explicit hint she could give on the public road.
Liang Shanbo heard that the younger sister loved reading, and he was immediately interested: "Since she's Zhu brother's sister, I'm sure she's a good person."
"Not just good," Zhu Yingtai said, "you might not even recognize her."
Liang Shanbo thought this was an exaggeration, asking if she had often changed her clothes as a child. Zhu Yingtai was silent for a long time, finally only reminding him to visit soon.

Liang Shanbo was worried about being too forward and asked what kind of gift his future sister-in-law would like. Zhu Yingtai replied that she didn't want jewels or precious stones, but only for him to remember their conversations on the road. Liang Shanbo repeated everything they had talked about, from the swans to the butterflies and the reflection in the well, but still didn't connect it to the person in front of him. Zhu Yingtai felt both comforted and anxious, saying, "You remember everything, but you still haven't understood – Liang Shanbo, this essay of yours needs to be rewritten."
Liang Shanbo smiled, saying, "Then please have the younger sister teach me in person."

(At this point, Liang Shanbo looked up at the academy gate, a hint of unease in his eyes, as if he was worried he would be mistaken for a stranger by the gatekeeper. The gatekeeper was busy sorting books, holding a large turtle that was tapping on the pages with its claws, making a "click-click" sound. Liang Shanbo couldn't help but laugh, and Zhu Yingtai smiled awkwardly, as if to say, "This turtle is really good at acting.")

Liang Shanbo continued, "I just want you to read the poem I wrote, and maybe it can help me connect the images with you." Zhu Yingtai nodded and handed him a piece of paper, and Liang Shanbo took it, looking up at the stone steps of the academy, where ancient poems were inscribed, and the vines below seemed to sway gently to their conversation. As Zhu Yingtai read the poem, her voice was clear and melodious, like the ripples on the pond. Liang Shanbo listened with a soft gaze, but he couldn't bring himself to look directly at Zhu Yingtai's eyes, fearing that they held too many unspoken secrets.
